accroche: Every mitochondrion carries a genome separate from the nucleus, in a loop, the signature of a bacterium that never left the cell that swallowed it.
contenu_vulgarise:
Every cell in your body contains a second genome, cut off from the one in the nucleus, laid out in a loop rather than in linear chromosomes, like that of a bacterium. This is not an isolated anomaly: it is the rule, in the mitochondria that produce the cell's energy, and in the chloroplasts that capture it in plants.

The idea that these are literally captured bacteria goes back to 1905: the Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowsky published, on September 15, a text proposing that chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria that were once free-living, swallowed by a host cell without being digested. He coined the word “symbiogenesis” for it. The hypothesis then faded for decades, marginal, until a young American biologist, Lynn Margulis, then signing as Lynn Sagan, revived it in 1967 in a paper, “On the Origin of Mitosing Cells.” The text was turned down by more than a dozen journals before finding refuge in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

## What the Genome Confirms

Margulis argued there that three cellular structures descend from free-living organisms swallowed by an ancestral cell: mitochondria, chloroplasts, and the basal bodies of flagella, the latter derived, in her view, from spiral-shaped bacteria close to spirochetes.

Two of the three hold up perfectly today. The mitochondria's own genome ties them to the alpha-proteobacteria; that of chloroplasts, to the cyanobacteria, the lineage Mereschkowsky had guessed without proof, a century before sequencing could verify it. Bacterial-type ribosomes, a double membrane inherited from the original engulfment, division independent of the rest of the cell: every detail points to the same conclusion. These two organelles did not appear in the cell; they entered it, and never left.

## The Third That Did Not Hold

The third part has never been confirmed. A flagellum contains no DNA and shows no structural resemblance to a bacterium, the exact opposite of what is observed for mitochondria and chloroplasts. This part of the hypothesis remains largely discarded today.

This uneven fate is, in a sense, the most instructive point of the story. A theory rejected fifteen times before publication ended up becoming one of the best-established facts of cell biology, without each of its parts surviving at the same pace. Science did not have to choose between proving Margulis right and proving her wrong: it did both, organelle by organelle, as genomes delivered their evidence.

repere.texte: The mitochondria's own genome ties them to the lineage of alpha-proteobacteria; that of chloroplasts, to the lineage of cyanobacteria, the double genomic signature that confirms the bacterial origin of both organelles.
repere.source: Gray, Michael W., “Lynn Margulis and the endosymbiont hypothesis: 50 years later,” Molecular Biology of the Cell, 2017

carte.punch: Your mitochondria have their own genome. That is no accident.
carte.idee: The looped genome of mitochondria and chloroplasts ties them to the alpha-proteobacteria and the cyanobacteria: these organelles were free-living bacteria, swallowed and never expelled. The idea, rejected fifteen times before its publication in 1967, is now well established.
carte.source_courte: M. W. Gray, Molecular Biology of the Cell, 2017

quiz.question: Why is Margulis's hypothesis about the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts now considered confirmed?
choix: Because ancient fossils of these organelles have been found in a totally free-living state
Because their own looped genome ties them phylogenetically to specific bacterial lineages
Because Margulis managed to recreate the phenomenon entirely in the laboratory
Because no other explanation has ever been seriously proposed for these organelles
quiz.explication: The decisive evidence comes from sequencing: the genome of mitochondria ties them to the alpha-proteobacteria, that of chloroplasts to the cyanobacteria. Bacterial-type ribosomes and a double membrane confirm the picture. The flagella hypothesis, by contrast, was discarded for lack of DNA in these structures.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the botanist Konstantin Mereschkowsky propose in 1905?
choix: That chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria that were once free-living, swallowed without being digested
That mitochondria descend from viruses that infected the ancestral cell
That all plant and animal cells share the same bacterial genome
That photosynthesis appeared independently in each plant lineage
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mereschkowsky published on September 15, 1905 a text proposing that chloroplasts descend from cyanobacteria that were once free-living, swallowed by a host cell without being digested; he coined the word symbiogenesis for it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What reception does Lynn Margulis's paper, then signed Lynn Sagan, receive in 1967?
choix: It is published immediately and hailed by the entire scientific community
It is published only after the author's death, posthumously
It is rejected by more than a dozen journals before being published
It is withdrawn from publication at the author's own request
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The paper, “On the Origin of Mitosing Cells,” was turned down by more than a dozen journals before finding refuge in the Journal of Theoretical Biology, where it finally appeared in 1967.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was the hypothesis about the basal bodies of flagella not confirmed?
choix: Because flagella disappear in most of the organisms studied
Because a flagellum contains no DNA and structurally resembles no bacterium
Because Margulis herself retracted this part of her hypothesis before 1970
Because the spirochetes proposed as ancestors have since gone extinct
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A flagellum contains no DNA and shows no structural resemblance to a bacterium, the exact opposite of what is observed for mitochondria and chloroplasts: this part of the hypothesis remains discarded.
